interactions.summary: A viewer asks what happens to Putin's long-term project if he dies or is removed and whether anyone in Russia would continue the same ideology after him.

Jiang predicts Putin will live another twenty years, then argues that after a great leader dies Russia would move from succession struggle into outward military expansion before eventually exhausting and decaying.
A student asks why each person is born as a specific self in a specific place and whether that has anything to do with the monad.

Jiang answers with a spiritual model: the soul chooses a purpose before birth, enters the world in the place needed to pursue that purpose, and must trust intuition through obstacles because life is part of a samsaric cycle of repeated attempts at enlightenment.
The lecture ends with a brief off-mic group goodbye after Jiang's closing thanks and YouTube sign-off.

speaker_notes.note: The final 'Bye' repetitions are off-mic and unattributed; they appear to be a mixed room response rather than a single identifiable speaker.

claims.claim: Jiang predicts that Putin will remain alive and in play for roughly another twenty years, framing that as an instinctive forecast rather than a demonstrated certainty.
He says that when a great leader dies, the first recurring pattern is internal friction as factions fight over succession.
Jiang argues that after succession conflict, elites may redirect internal struggle outward by launching wars of expansion because they cannot agree internally and seek unity through conquest.
He predicts that post-Putin Russia could spend ten to twenty years conquering outward because few neighboring societies are as militarized as Russia.
Jiang says the long-run result of that expansion is exhaustion: whether Russia wins or loses, the empire eventually decays because it fights too many wars at once.
He says he does not see Russia as having a great future because the historical pattern after a strong leader's death is friction, expansion, and then exhaustion.
Jiang presents a spiritual anthropology in which a soul comes to Earth with a chosen purpose, and that purpose is fundamentally a path toward enlightenment.
He says a person is assigned to a particular place and identity because that placement best enables the soul to pursue its chosen purpose.
Jiang says parents, schools, and society often block people from knowing or pursuing their purpose, but those obstacles are themselves part of the soul's developmental path.
He frames repeated earthly return as samsara: if a soul does not fulfill its purpose, it returns to try again under a new purpose until it understands itself more fully.
Jiang advises students to trust intuition because even if they cannot remember their purpose explicitly, they can feel it, and that felt intuition is what leads them toward it.
He concludes that both the students' presence in the classroom and his own teaching role are part of purpose, presenting this as the underlying structure of the universe.

signature_moments.moment: After a great leader dies, Jiang's cycle is not peaceful succession but panic, outward war, and expansion as a substitute for agreement.
signature_moments.source_phrase: we cannot possibly agree on succession. So what we'll do is we will just go to war with everyone
signature_moments.why_it_matters: It is the packet's sharpest political mechanism and the hinge between the Putin question and Jiang's wider imperial theory.

signature_moments.moment: The empire's end is not heroic victory but exhaustion, parallel decay, and overextension.
signature_moments.source_phrase: everyone's exhausted and then they just decay in parallel
signature_moments.why_it_matters: It preserves the packet's clearest image of how conquest turns back into decline.

signature_moments.moment: Identity is answered with a purpose-driven cosmology: the soul chooses a mission, enters the world where that mission can be worked out, and meets obstacles as part of the assignment.
signature_moments.source_phrase: you come to Earth as a soul, and your soul has a purpose
signature_moments.why_it_matters: This is the final lecture's strongest metaphysical compression and shifts the exam from geopolitics into spiritual anthropology.

signature_moments.moment: Purpose is not mainly remembered conceptually; it is felt, and intuition is the practical guide back toward it.
signature_moments.source_phrase: you can feel what your purpose is
signature_moments.why_it_matters: It captures the practical directive Jiang leaves the class with instead of reducing the ending to abstract reincarnation talk.

glossary_terms.definition_or_usage: The post-leader moment when internal factions fight over who inherits power, which Jiang sees as the trigger for later outward war.
Jiang's term for the phase after imperial overexpansion when victory or defeat matters less than total depletion and parallel decay.
The pre-birth mission Jiang says organizes a person's identity, placement, obstacles, and path toward enlightenment.
Named here as the Vedic-psychology cycle in which a soul returns repeatedly when it fails to complete its purpose.
The felt inner guidance Jiang says reveals purpose even when explicit memory of that purpose is absent.

chronology_notes.note: This 2026-05-28 packet gives Jiang's dated post-Putin sequence in full: long leader survival, succession friction, outward conquest, then exhaustion and decay.

The lecture's closing move on 2026-05-28 shifts from geopolitical forecast into a metaphysical model of soul purpose, samsara, and intuition, so later read-writing should preserve that tonal pivot rather than treating the ending as throwaway outro.

uncertainty_notes.note: The student asks whether this is connected to 'Mona,' which is likely an ASR distortion of a prior metaphysical term such as monad; the semantic pass preserves the identity-purpose question without over-correcting the noun.
The final goodbye is extremely brief and unattributed, so it is kept as a low-stakes closing exchange rather than assigned to a single speaker.
